questions.prompt: A brittle ionic crystal fractures when stress shifts one layer relative to the next. Which particulate explanation is consistent with this behavior?
options: The shift removes the charges from every ion, so all electrostatic interactions disappear.
The shift changes every cation into an anion without changing the electron distribution.
The ions become discrete neutral molecules whose covalent bonds all break.
The shift can bring like-charged ions next to one another, creating repulsions that favor fracture.
questions.explanation: D is correct. An ionic lattice is stabilized by its arrangement of positive and negative ions. A layer displacement can align like charges, producing strong repulsive interactions and brittleness. A incorrectly neutralizes ions merely by moving them. B changes ionic charge without the required electron transfer. C replaces the ionic array with a molecular model. Fracture changes the arrangement and separation of charged particles; it does not require every ion to become neutral.

questions.prompt: Diamond is a three-dimensional covalent network, whereas solid I2 consists of discrete I2 molecules. Why is diamond much more resistant to deformation in the introductory structure model?
options: Deforming its rigid network requires disrupting strong directional covalent interactions, whereas neighboring I2 molecules are held together by weaker intermolecular interactions.
Diamond consists of individual carbon molecules with stronger dispersion forces solely because carbon atoms are lighter.
I2 must contain an ionic lattice because iodine atoms have many electrons.
Every covalent substance must be harder than every noncovalent solid, independent of its network or layer structure.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Diamond’s fixed three-dimensional network resists rearrangement through strong covalent connections. I2 molecules retain internal covalent bonds but interact with neighboring molecules mainly through dispersion. B incorrectly makes diamond molecular and treats smaller mass as a cause of stronger dispersion. C equates a large electron count with ionic bonding. D makes an unjustified universal rule; layered graphite, for example, illustrates why connectivity and directions of interaction matter. The conclusion here concerns the specified structures, not a ranking based only on the word covalent.

questions.prompt: A dry solid composite contains NaCl crystals and a continuous connected copper network bridging two electrodes. It conducts electricity while the NaCl remains crystalline. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The conductivity proves that every ion in the NaCl crystals can migrate freely; the copper network is irrelevant.
The copper must be an insulator because particles can carry electrical charge only after a solid melts.
Mobile delocalized electrons in the connected copper network can account for the current without requiring the NaCl ions to migrate.
Current must be carried by neutral NaCl formula units moving through the fixed copper network.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The connected metallic network provides a path for mobile electronic charge carriers, even while the ionic component remains a nonconducting crystal. A incorrectly transfers a property of the whole composite to every component and ignores the explicit metallic path. B contradicts metallic solid-state conduction. D assigns charge transport to neutral formula units rather than identifying mobile charged particles. Conductivity of a multicomponent solid does not, by itself, prove that each component conducts or that the ionic lattice has melted.

questions.prompt: A sample of molecular solid CO2 sublimes to CO2 gas without chemical decomposition. Which interactions are primarily overcome as molecules separate?
options: The C=O covalent bonds within every molecule.
The intermolecular attractions between intact CO2 molecules.
Covalent bonds connecting different CO2 units throughout a continuous carbon–oxygen network.
The ionic attractions between separate C4+ and O2- ions in a CO2 lattice.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Sublimation separates intact molecules by overcoming intermolecular cohesion. A would break the CO2 molecules into different chemical species, contradicting the stated absence of decomposition. C incorrectly treats molecular solid CO2 as a covalent network connecting different CO2 units. D imposes an ionic lattice on a molecular solid. The internal C=O bonds remain present in both the solid and gas; a physical phase change need not sever covalent bonds within the molecules.

questions.prompt: Two molecular solids have different melting points. A student concludes that the solid with the higher melting point must have stronger covalent bonds inside its molecules. Which evaluation is best?
options: The conclusion follows because melting always breaks every covalent bond inside each molecule.
The conclusion follows because a melting point is a direct measurement of an individual bond energy.
The conclusion fails only if one sample contains more total grams than the other.
The conclusion is unsupported: intermolecular interactions and crystal packing can affect melting without breaking the intramolecular bonds.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Melting molecular solids rearranges the interactions between molecules; differences in packing and intermolecular cohesion affect the transition. A confuses melting with chemical decomposition. B treats a bulk phase-transition temperature as a direct isolated-bond measurement. C confuses total sample mass with the structural factors controlling a melting point. A higher melting point alone does not establish stronger internal covalent bonds, and melting trends can be more subtle than a simple force-strength ranking.

questions.prompt: Two stable molecular liquids P and Q have similar molecular sizes and shapes, but P has stronger net intermolecular attractions. At the same temperature where both remain liquids, which qualitative prediction is appropriate?
options: P has a higher vapor pressure and a lower normal boiling point.
P and Q must have identical vapor pressures because their molecules have similar sizes.
P generally has a lower vapor pressure and a higher normal boiling point.
P must decompose into ions before any molecules enter the vapor.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Stronger cohesion generally makes escape into the vapor less favorable at a given temperature, lowering equilibrium vapor pressure. More heating is then needed for its vapor pressure to reach the same external pressure, giving a higher boiling point. A reverses both trends. B omits the stated difference in interactions. D substitutes chemical ion formation for vaporization of a stable molecular liquid. The prediction is the usual qualitative model for comparable liquids, not a claim that size alone fixes their properties.

questions.prompt: An unknown solid has a high melting point and does not conduct electricity while solid. Is this evidence alone sufficient to distinguish an ionic solid from a three-dimensional covalent network solid?
options: No; both can fit these observations, so additional structural or appropriate conductivity evidence is needed.
Yes; every nonconducting solid with a high melting point must be ionic.
Yes; every ionic solid conducts electricity before melting.
No; neither type can have a high melting point.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Many ionic solids and three-dimensional network solids have strong interactions, high melting points, and poor solid-state conductivity. The observations do not uniquely identify one structure. B overstates the diagnostic power of two shared properties. C ignores the limited mobility of ions in an ionic crystal. D reverses the expected effect of strong interactions. Appropriate additional evidence could include a structural model or molten conductivity where the material can be melted and remains chemically stable; no single unsafe or universally feasible experiment is prescribed.

questions.prompt: Heating changes a protein’s shape and its ability to bind another molecule, while analysis shows that its covalent backbone remains intact. Which explanation is consistent with this observation?
options: The loss of binding proves that every peptide bond in the backbone was broken.
Noncovalent contacts that help stabilize its folded shape were disrupted or rearranged, changing its binding geometry.
The unchanged backbone proves that all three-dimensional interactions and the shape remained unchanged.
Only the protein’s total molecular mass determines binding; its folded shape cannot matter.
questions.explanation: B is correct. A biomolecule’s function can depend on its three-dimensional arrangement, which is supported by many noncovalent contacts. Rearranging those contacts can change binding even while the covalent backbone stays intact. A contradicts the stated intact covalent backbone and confuses loss of folded structure with cleavage of every peptide bond. C ignores noncovalent interactions beyond the backbone. D excludes the geometric and chemical fit of a binding site and incorrectly treats total mass as sufficient to determine binding. The observation does not specify one universal unfolding pathway; it supports a structure/function explanation involving noncovalent interactions.

questions.prompt: Graphite has strong covalent bonding within carbon sheets but is soft and can leave layers on paper. Which feature of its structure explains the softness?
options: Every carbon atom is an independent nonbonded particle with no covalent neighbors.
The strong bonds within each sheet must all break whenever two sheets slide.
Adjacent sheets can slide relative to one another because interlayer attractions are weaker than the covalent connections within a sheet.
Graphite is an ionic solid whose layers contain alternating C4+ and C4- ions.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Graphite’s layered structure is strongly bonded within sheets but more weakly held between them, allowing relative layer motion. A erases the two-dimensional covalent network. B incorrectly requires breaking the within-sheet network for interlayer sliding. D substitutes unsupported full ionic charges for covalently connected carbon. The example shows why a material’s properties depend on the dimensional arrangement of interactions as well as their type.

questions.prompt: An interstitial alloy is less easily bent than its pure metallic host but still conducts electricity. Which combination of microscopic features can account for both observations?
options: Small added atoms hinder structural rearrangement, while the alloy retains mobile delocalized electrons.
Small added atoms obstruct deformation, but electrical current is carried by metal cores migrating through the solid.
The alloy becomes a fixed ionic lattice whose stationary charged particles carry electrical current without moving.
The added atoms make the host layers slide more freely, while all electrons become permanently localized.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Interstitial atoms can increase rigidity by obstructing rearrangement of the metal structure, yet metallic delocalized electrons can remain available for conduction. B can account for rigidity but incorrectly assigns ordinary solid-metal current to migrating cores. C replaces metallic bonding with an ionic lattice and then supplies no mobile charge carrier; stationary charges do not carry a current through the material. D predicts easier bending and reduced electronic mobility, opposite to the stated combination. Mechanical resistance and electrical conduction depend on related but different aspects of the structure; one does not force the other to disappear.

questions.prompt: A molecular solid melts into a cohesive liquid without decomposition. A student draws the liquid with widely separated molecules experiencing no intermolecular attractions. What is the main defect in this model?
options: The liquid’s volume can be explained only by each molecule becoming physically larger.
Liquid molecules remain close together and interacting; melting rearranges their contacts rather than eliminating all intermolecular cohesion.
The liquid must contain isolated atoms because melting destroys molecular identity.
The liquid molecules must occupy perfectly fixed repeating lattice positions.
questions.explanation: B is correct. A liquid retains close neighbors and significant interparticle attractions while allowing molecules to change relative positions. A attributes bulk phase behavior entirely to individual molecules swelling rather than to their relative arrangements and motion. C contradicts the absence of decomposition. D retains the fixed crystalline arrangement of a solid. Complete removal of cohesive interactions is a useful contrast for a widely separated gas model, not for the dense liquid described here. Melting can therefore be more sensitive to rearrangement and packing than a simple all-forces-removed picture.
